category: relay (WebSocket to raw TCP, self-operated deployment)

free_tier.stated: no price is published for the relay itself. Forward tokens are self-minted with no account, and reverse pairs are self-created with no account, so a caller pays nothing to use it. Its own cost is the Cloudflare Worker, Durable Object and Workers VPC bill of the account that deploys it, and that figure is not published
free_tier.notes: the specification closes with 'Cost: check current Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, and Workers VPC pricing before changing scale assumptions', which is a documented absence of a cost figure

per_object_cap.stated: 64 MiB per session in both directions combined, enforced by a close with code 1009 and reason 'session byte cap'
per_object_cap.notes: measured: a 67,107,029-byte download stopped at 64.0 MiB with close 1009 'session byte cap' after 6.66 s

retention.stated: a forward token lives at most 72 hours from minting; a reverse pair and its three tokens live at most 72 hours. Expiry is checked when a session is established, not per frame
retention.notes: Forward token lifetime and reverse pair lifetime both measured at 72.0 hours on 2026-10-22.

egress.terms: the caller's traffic leaves through the relay's own address, not the caller's. Six colos answered with six distinct addresses, all inside Cloudflare's 104.28.0.0/16. Every session took the vpc road

tooling: Any RFC 6455 client. Forward path: wss://<host>/connect/<target-host>/<port>. Reverse path: wss://<host>/v1/node/<name> for the node and wss://<host>/v1/connect/<name> for the remote connection.
interface_detail: forward: WebSocket upgrade on /connect/<host>/<port> with a forward token in X-Relay-Token, then binary frames carry raw TCP bytes both ways. reverse: /v1/pair mints a name and three tokens, /v1/node/<name> for the node, /v1/connect/<name> for the operator, /v1/status/<name> and POST /v1/stop/<name> for control
chaining: the sealed-sandbox reach-in: a host that cannot bind a port dials out to /v1/node, an operator dials /v1/connect, and the pair is joined by a 128-bit name. It composes after a sandbox whose inbound policy is unpublished, and it does not compose with bulk serving because 64 MiB per session is the cap.

limits.value: 64 MiB per session, both directions combined; the relay closes with 1009 'session byte cap'
262,144 bytes per WebSocket frame on the forward path, and 65,568 bytes per operator frame on the reverse path (32-byte session id plus 65,536 payload)
a session caps at 720 minutes and 64 MiB; an idle session closes after 180,000 ms of payload inactivity and transport keepalives do not reset that clock

120 admissions per minute from one address, applied only to unauthenticated forward WebSocket attempts and to public mint and pair creation. Authenticated sessions, authenticated reverse requests and diagnostics do not share that bucket
reverse path only: 1 MiB of queued bytes per receiver, past which the relay drops the undelivered frame and closes 1011 'relay backpressure'
one name holds one node socket: a second node connection on the same name is refused with HTTP 409 before accept

limits_note: The 64 MiB session cap and 720-minute session life were measured or read in documentation on 2026-10-22. The 180,000 ms idle close was measured at 180.7 s. At 9.605 MiB/s sustained, moving 1 TiB in 24 hours requires 16,384 sessions of 64 MiB, or one new session every 5.3 seconds. The 64 MiB cap applies per session.
binding_note: the 64 MiB per-session cap binds before the rate and before the clock: a session can carry 64 MiB and then must be replaced, so the volume a reader can move is a session count rather than a bandwidth figure. The 720-minute life binds only workloads that are idle rather than full.

identity_cost.detail: no account, no card and no email: POST /v1/mint returns a forward token and POST /v1/pair returns a name with a node, connect and stop token. The token is the identity, and the relay authenticates tokens rather than people

reliability_note: No reliability event recorded. Both tokens on a reverse pair and the forward token are bearer credentials, so anyone who reads one can open a session, and the relay carries the plaintext byte stream it forwards.
confidence_note: the version, the 37-entry pool, the policy block, the six per-colo egress addresses, the forward banner, the 64 MiB session cap, the 180 s idle close, the 72 h token life and both transports were measured from this host on 2026-10-22. The 720-minute session cap and the 120/minute admission brake are documented on the relay's own specification and were not measured, so the record's weakest rung is measured for the fields the verdict rests on and documented for those two

evidence.proved: 200, 1,436 bytes, sha256 31c2de2d146b2c488b2a382e1789b05ef2ec894bd95499cb315f4f802bb5b320: version 2026-10-03-r2, a 37-entry pool, reverse enabled, and policy token_required true with max_frame_bytes 262144

seven colos, seven distinct observed egress addresses: default 104.28.196.82, aws:eu-central-1 104.28.197.9, gcp:us-central1 104.28.248.184, aws:us-east-1 104.28.196.79, aws:eu-west-3 104.28.211.192, aws:ap-south-1 104.28.200.92, azure:westeurope 104.28.219.140, all address_family 6 and all egress.road vpc
the relay dialed github.com:22 at 140.82.121.3 over the vpc road, connect 0 ms, first byte 255 ms, 18 bytes seen, verdict live, banner SSH-2.0-6615c807

a raw WebSocket client that is not dropssh opened the forward session, sent HTTP/1.1 and read 1,010 bytes back in three binary frames beginning 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK', then close 1000 'target closed'. The forward path delivers the client's own bytes, not only the target's greeting

the target's 18-byte SSH banner arrived before any client byte, then the 15-byte client identification string drew 824 bytes of key-exchange payload, so a whole SSH handshake is deliverable in both directions over the forward path

a 67,107,029-byte download stopped at exactly 64.0 MiB with close 1009 'session byte cap' after 6.66 s, which is 9.605 MiB/s sustained to the cap. This is the measurement of the documented per-session byte cap
a forward session held open with no payload after the greeting closed after 180.7 s with close 1001 'idle timeout', which is the documented 180,000 ms idle close measured for the first time

a node that is not dropbear and not SSH answered the relay's hello, open and close controls, sent ready and one data frame, and an operator on /v1/connect read its 44 bytes back. The reverse transport is not SSH-specific

18,359 bytes, sha256 88eb1b0b8571b829daab17614ea2e27966ba5611951ea28db84660fc41cfa5a8: session caps of 720 min and 64 MiB, an idle close at 180,000 ms of payload inactivity, a 120/minute address brake on unauthenticated forward and public mint and pair calls, a 72 h token life, a 4 KiB control-frame cap, a 1 MiB backpressure queue, and the statement that no cost figure is published
3,595 bytes, sha256 7907c56dabb4739e03b7bddb0589faaaf9660d4ced4c647cab2208819abd5d30: the short form of the same contract

three placements returned the same egress address as the seed's 2026-10-02 measurement: aws:ap-south-1 104.28.200.92, aws:eu-central-1 104.28.197.9, aws:us-east-1 104.28.196.79. The client-nearest default differs, 104.28.204.8 then against 104.28.196.82 now

notes: Version 2026-10-03-r2 measured with a 37-entry pool on 2026-10-22. The forward path is wss://<host>/connect/<target-host>/<port>; the reverse path is wss://<host>/v1/node/<name>.

extras.sessions_for_one_tib_note: 16384: 1 TiB divided by the measured 64 MiB session cap. At 9.605 MiB/s a session reaches the cap in 6.66 s, so replacing sessions back to back is the limiting operation rather than bandwidth, and one day at that rate is 16,384 of them, or one new session every 5.3 seconds

seed_colo_comparison.note: the seed measured the same three named placements on 2026-10-02 and every one returned the same address on 2026-10-22, twenty days later. Only the default colo differs, and it is the client-nearest one, so a different caller edge colo is the expected explanation.
seed_colo_comparison.what_it_settles: the seed's review R4 recorded that one probe per colo could not establish that a colo's egress is stable over time. Two probes twenty days apart on three named placements now show it is, and the default colo's difference is consistent with the caller's edge colo having changed rather than the relay's address
seed_colo_comparison.what_it_does_not_settle: ?spread= within one colo, and whether the address survives a relay redeploy. Two points are not a series.

extras.transit_note: the relay copies the byte stream it forwards in both directions, measured at 64 MiB per session
